newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgians march in white for justice.
newsitem.headline: Belgians march in white for justice.

text.p: Belgians massed on Brussels on Sunday waving white balloons and flowers in an outpouring of anger against their political and judicial system.
"Ashamed to be Belgian" read one marcher's banners, summing up feelings which have swept the country since the lurid tale of child kidnapping, sex abuse and murder exploded in August.

Led by the parents and relatives of missing or dead children, suspected to be the victims of a child sex gang, a tide of people wearing or carrying white swept down a boulevard in the centre of the capital.
Estimates of the crowd ranged from 250,000 to 325,000.

Many came on to the streets for the first time, feeling a need to voice their concern over a law and order system seen as corrupt and unable to protect ordinary Belgians and their children in particular, from crime.

Gerda Zammattio, who brought her three-year-old daughter Naomi from the town of Mechelen to join the march: "I am here to show solidarity with the parents. What has happened in the last few weeks moved me greatly. The system must become more humane."

But in the main the cries for justice were silent, in line with the wishes of the parents and relatives of four girls whose bodies have been unearthed since mid-August when police uncovered a child sex, kidnap and murder ring.

Two other girls were sexually abused, but rescued from the gang, alleged to have been led by Marc Dutroux, a convicted child rapist released 10 years early in 1992 from a 13-year sentence for multiple child rape.
Dutroux is one of 13 people charged in connection with the case. Scores of videos with child porn were seized.

The marchers, large numbers of parents with their own children, had adopted white as a symbol of hope, turning the three km (two mile) march route between the North and South Stations into a sea of white balloons bobbing in a chill wind.

Tempers flared at the South Station when it became clear to the crowd that from placards with 15 names of the dead girls and others suspected of having fallen into the hands of criminals the name of a missing young Morroccan girl was absent.
There were cries of "Loubna, we will not forget you."
But most demonstrators simply laid their flowers in front of the billboard-size placards and went into the station to try and catch a train home.
The parents and relatives went on to a closed-door meeting with Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene in his official residence.

After the meeting Nabella Benaissa, sister of Loubna, said Dehaene had made four promises, including the creation of an independent national centre for missing and exploited children before the end of the year.
He also pledged that everything would be done to ensure the investigation into the deaths of the four girls would be thorough and the truth be brought to light.
"It was quite a concrete meeting," Benaissa said.
Towards the end of the afternoon a breakaway group of several thousand marchers headed for the Justice Palace where they were met by barricades, police and water cannons.

Throwing firecrackers, eggs, stones and marbles, the group of mainly students loudly voiced their anger at judges and magistrates whom they said had lost touch with reality, but there were no clashes with police.

The Palais de Justice had been a prominent target in the past of week of protests which broke out spontaneously after Belgium's top court removed a popular magistrate from investigations into the ring.
The court ruled magistrate Jean-Marc Connerotte had compromised himself by accepting a free dinner from a support group specialising in helping the parents of missing children.
The ruling, following the letter rather than the spirit of the law, prompted an already morally-outraged public to take to the streets and call for a clean-up of the justice system.
